data.title: EU presidency proposes 8% cut to 2028-2034 EU budget to €1.6 trillion
data.description:
The European Union's long-term budget for 2028-2034 should be 8% lower than the European Commission's proposed €2 trillion, the Irish EU presidency said on Saturday.

This would result in a budget of €1.6 trillion, subject to contentious negotiations among EU countries in the coming months. The EU budget is the main source of financing for all of the 27-country bloc's main policies.

data.title: Tom Lee Says Stocks Are A ‘Coiled Spring’ As AI Skepticism Peaks — ‘Rates Are No Longer A Negative Story’
data.description:
Key points:
  • Lee said recent market action is a reminder of just how sensitive equities have become to developments surrounding AI, with even seemingly minor headlines capable of triggering outsized reactions.
  • He pointed to oil prices and interest rates as two of the biggest sources of potential pain for stocks.
  • At the same time, he said investor sentiment toward the AI boom has become increasingly pessimistic.

Fundstrat Managing Partner Tom Lee on Friday said that he sees a potential stock market rebound taking shape as investors grow increasingly skeptical of the artificial intelligence boom and worry about elevated interest rates.

During an interview with CNBC, Lee described equities as a "coiled spring," arguing that the very factors weighing on stocks today, including AI pessimism and high borrowing costs, could eventually fuel a reversal.

Lee Sees A ‘Coiled Spring’ In Stocks

Lee said recent market action is a reminder of just how sensitive equities have become to developments surrounding AI, with even seemingly minor headlines capable of triggering outsized reactions.

But rather than viewing that sensitivity as purely bearish, Lee sees it as evidence that the market could be positioned for a reversal.

"I think yesterday and today are examples of why this market is a coiled spring on the negative side," Lee said.

He pointed to oil prices and interest rates as two of the biggest sources of potential pain for stocks. At the same time, he said investor sentiment toward the AI boom has become increasingly pessimistic.

"I've been meeting with investors on the road since September 28th, and investors are very skeptical of this AI boom," Lee said, while adding that many investors now view AI as a bubble.

That skepticism could ultimately become a contrarian catalyst if upcoming developments fail to validate the bearish narrative, he added.

Why Lee Thinks AI Earnings Could Change The Mood

Lee expects third-quarter (Q3) earnings to provide an important test for the AI trade and potentially restore investor confidence.

"I'm going to be in a camp that third-quarter earnings… it’s going to restore the confidence of AI," Lee said.

The setup is particularly important because concerns about AI have increasingly centered on the amount of capital being committed to the technology, the cost of funding that spending and whether the returns will justify it.

Lee doesn't necessarily see the concentration of AI investment as a warning sign. “I'd rather see a few companies driving the spending,” he said.

In his view, having a relatively small number of dominant companies leading AI investment can actually demonstrate where competitive advantages and economic moats are being created.

Lee also expects the upcoming U.S. midterm elections to remove some of the political uncertainty surrounding AI stocks. Once the elections are behind investors, Lee believes political pressure on AI companies could ease, even if Democrats take control of the Senate.

Why Lee Says Rates May No Longer Be A Threat To Stocks

The other major piece of Lee's bullish case is interest rates. With Treasury yields elevated, bonds and Treasury inflation-protected securities are increasingly competing with equities for investor capital.

But Lee believes the rate surge may be approaching a point where it becomes difficult for yields to move substantially higher.

"We're reaching sort of the peak point there," Lee said.

He pointed to record commercial short positions in Treasuries and the economic impact of elevated borrowing costs as reasons to believe the rate move could be nearing its limits.

Higher rates are already weakening capital demand, Lee said, because some companies can no longer justify issuing debt at current levels. If rates eventually move lower, the impact on equities could be significant.

"I think we're at the point here where rates are no longer a negative story for equities," he said.

During the after-hours session on Friday, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), which tracks the S&P 500 index, was flat; the Invesco QQQ Trust ETF (QQQ) edged up by 0.01%; and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) rose 0.02%. Retail sentiment on Stocktwits toward the S&P 500 ETF was in the ‘bullish’ territory at the time of writing.

data.title: Thailand prepares to host IMF-World Bank meetings
data.description:
Thailand is preparing to host the IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok from October 12–18, bringing together more than 15,000 participants from 191 countries, including central bank governors, economic policymakers and business leaders, for discussions on the world economy.

  • To ease traffic, Bangkok government offices will work from home on October 12, 14 and 15, while October 13 is an existing public holiday and October 16 has been declared a special government and bank holiday, with private companies and state enterprises asked to consider suitable arrangements.

  • Security has been tightened at the meeting venue in central Bangkok and 21 official hotels, according to the authorities.

  • About 500 Tourist Police officers will also help secure the venue, delegate hotels and tourist attractions through undercover deployments, patrols, drones and motorcade escorts coordinated with around 39 embassies, Tourist Police Bureau Commissioner Phongsiam Meekhanthong said.

  • Visiting leaders include Swiss President Guy Parmelin, making the first official visit to Thailand by a Swiss president in 22 years, and Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, the Thai Foreign Ministry said.

  • Participants’ spending could generate 1.05–2.25 billion baht for the Thai economy, according to the Thai Finance Ministry.

  • More than 320 electric vehicles will serve participants to cut carbon emissions, the Thai Finance Ministry said.

  • Heavy to very heavy rain is forecast for Bangkok and surrounding provinces on October 10–11, potentially causing localised flooding, the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration warned. This comes after parts of the city flooded two weeks ago following 320 mm (12.6 inches) of rain over three days.

data.title: The Defining Skill For The Future Is Adaptability: BIAL’s Nalini George
data.description:
With internal job posting participation up over 200 per cent and women's participation up seven-fold, the CHRO explains how transparent career pathways and AI capability building are preparing a multi-employer airport workforce for expansion

At Bangalore International Airport Limited (BIAL), the workforce is being asked to absorb two large changes together: a bigger airport and a more AI-driven way of running it. Real-time AI now supports passenger flow, cargo and operations, and the people behind them include security staff, ground handlers, cargo teams and data scientists, employed by multiple organisations on one campus.

Nalini George, chief human resources officer (CHRO) at BIAL, who spent six years building talent strategy at Rakuten before moving into airport operations, treats the two as a single people agenda. In this conversation, she explains how frontline hiring is shifting towards digital fluency and adaptability, why BIAL keeps one consistent message on AI and jobs, and how a competency-based career framework has lifted internal job posting participation by over 200 per cent, with women's participation growing seven-fold.

BIAL is building itself into what the industry is calling an "algorithmic airport," running real-time AI across passenger flow, cargo and operations. Two years into the CHRO role, what has that shift changed about the skills you're hiring for on the frontline compared to what you inherited in 2024?

The shift to becoming an algorithmic airport has fundamentally changed how we think about talent. While operational excellence remains non-negotiable in a safety-critical environment, we are increasingly hiring for digital fluency, adaptability, and data-driven decision-making alongside traditional operational capabilities.

In the past, many frontline roles were primarily focused on process execution, compliance, and operational discipline. Today, those same roles require employees to work confidently with AI-powered systems, real-time operational dashboards, predictive insights, and intelligent automation that support everything from passenger flow and cargo movement to airport operations.

As a result, we place greater emphasis on individuals who are comfortable using technology, interpreting data, solving problems, and making decisions in dynamic environments. We are looking for people who can combine operational expertise with curiosity, learning agility, and the ability to adapt to rapidly changing ways of working.

What has been particularly striking is that the defining skill for the future is not coding, but adaptability. Technology will continue to evolve, but the ability to learn, unlearn, and relearn quickly will remain invaluable. That is why we have invested significantly in building AI and digital capabilities across our workforce, ensuring that technology adoption becomes part of everyday work rather than the domain of specialists alone.

In simple terms, we have evolved from hiring primarily for operational excellence to hiring for operational excellence combined with digital intelligence, continuous learning, and future readiness. The airports of the future will be powered by technology, but their success will ultimately depend on people who know how to harness it.

An airport workforce spans security staff, ground handlers, cargo teams and data scientists under one roof, groups that experience AI very differently day to day. How do you calibrate one message on AI and job security across a diverse workforce?

One of the most important lessons we have learned is that you cannot have a one-size-fits-all conversation about AI in an airport ecosystem. A security officer, a ground handler, a cargo professional, and a data scientist will experience AI very differently in their day-to-day work. What connects them, however, is a shared need to understand what AI means for their role and their future.

Our approach has been to keep one message consistent: AI is here to augment people, not replace them. The purpose of AI is to make work safer, simpler, faster, and more informed by taking over repetitive tasks and providing better insights, while leaving critical human judgment, expertise, empathy, and decision-making where they belong: with people.

At the same time, we recognise that the questions employees have are deeply personal. People are not asking whether AI will change work. They already know it will. What they want to know is, "What does this mean for me?" That is where transparency becomes critical. We have found that uncertainty creates anxiety, but understanding creates confidence.

That is why our focus has been as much on capability building as on technology deployment. We want every employee, regardless of role, to feel equipped to work alongside technology and confident about their ability to grow with it. The conversation is not about protecting jobs from AI. It is about preparing people for a future where technology becomes an increasingly powerful partner in their work.

Ultimately, airports will always be people businesses. Technology can help us move passengers more efficiently, improve safety, and make better decisions, but it is people who build trust, respond in moments of uncertainty, solve complex problems, and create memorable experiences. Our role as leaders is to ensure our employees see AI not as a threat to their future, but as a tool that helps them thrive in it.

You spent six years building talent strategy inside Rakuten, a business built natively around technology, before moving into a much older, more physical industry. What has that contrast taught you about how ready a traditional operations-heavy workforce is for AI, compared to a tech-native one?

Technology readiness and technology maturity are two very different things. One of the biggest lessons from moving from a technology-native company to an airport ecosystem is not to confuse proximity to technology with readiness for change.

At Rakuten, technology was native to the business. Employees lived and breathed digital innovation every day. At BIAL, the business is fundamentally operational and physical, but increasingly technology enabled. On the surface, those worlds appear very different. In reality, the people challenge is remarkably similar: how do you make technology meaningful for employees, build the right capabilities, and create a workforce that remains adaptable as the business evolves?

What I have found is that readiness for AI is less about the industry people work in and more about their mindset. Our frontline teams may not all be technologists, but they operate in an environment that demands constant adaptation. Every day, they respond to changing passenger volumes, operational complexities, safety requirements, and customer expectations. That adaptability is a powerful foundation for embracing new technologies.

The key is helping people see technology as a solution to real problems rather than technology for its own sake. Whether you are a security officer, a cargo specialist, an engineer, or a data scientist, people adopt new tools when they make work safer, simpler, faster, or more effective.

That is why our philosophy has remained consistent across environments: first fix the process, then use technology to make it better. AI is not a substitute for good processes or good people. It is an enabler that helps both perform at a higher level.

Ultimately, AI is not a technology strategy, it is a people strategy. The organisations that succeed will not necessarily be those with the most sophisticated algorithms, but those that create the confidence, capability, and culture needed for people to harness them. My experience across both technology and airport ecosystems has convinced me that when people are empowered to learn and adapt, industry becomes irrelevant. Human potential remains the greatest competitive advantage.

You've spoken about using data to guide career growth and using technology to challenge the status quo. What does that actually look like for someone in a ground operations role at BIAL, rather than a desk-based analyst, when you're mapping out their next skill path?

It starts with removing the idea that a career has to be a straight line.

For someone in ground operations, growth does not have to mean moving up within the same function. It could mean building deeper expertise, moving across functions, taking on new operational responsibilities, or progressing towards leadership. Programmes such as EXCEL (Our internal policy) help make those cross-functional opportunities more visible and accessible.

Our competency-based career framework shifts the conversation from “What is your current job?” to “What capabilities do you have, and what capabilities do you want to build?” That is important because the future of work will be shaped less by job titles and more by transferable skills.

Data helps us make that conversation practical. It allows us to identify capability gaps, understand emerging skill requirements, and create more personalized learning and career pathways. It also helps challenge traditional assumptions about who can move into which role and opens up opportunities that employees may not have previously considered.

The impact is already visible. We have seen Internal Job Posting participation increase over 200 per cent in the last few years, while women's participation has grown seven-fold, demonstrating that when opportunities become more transparent, people are far more willing to pursue them.

Ultimately, for an employee on the ground, career growth should not be limited by the function they started in. It should expand with the capabilities they build. Our role is to use data, technology, and development opportunities to create a career ecosystem where every employee can continuously learn, grow, and remain future-ready.

Your recent thinking on retention has centred on belonging over benefits. As AI automates more of the passenger and cargo experience, where does that sense of belonging get built for employees whose daily work is increasingly mediated by a screen or an algorithm rather than a person?

I have always believed that people stay because they feel they matter, not because they receive one more benefit. Benefits can support the employee’s experience, but belonging is what creates a lasting connection to an organisation.

As AI becomes more embedded in passenger services, cargo operations, and day-to-day decision-making, there is a natural concern that work could become more transactional or mediated by screens and algorithms. My view is exactly the opposite. The more technology advances, the more important the human experience becomes.

Belonging is not built through technology. It is built through purpose, growth, relationships, recognition, and the feeling that your contribution matters. AI can help employees work more efficiently, but it cannot replace the sense of pride someone feels when they solve a complex operational challenge, support a colleague during a critical moment, or contribute to creating a seamless experience for millions of passengers.

For us, the question is not how technology affects belonging, but how technology can create more space for it. If AI removes repetitive tasks, simplifies processes, or gives employees better information, it allows them to spend more time on the aspects of work that are uniquely human: collaboration, problem-solving, learning, innovation, and connection.

That is why we invest heavily in career growth, learning opportunities, leadership accessibility, cross-functional experiences, wellbeing, and community building. We want employees to see a future for themselves at BIAL and to feel connected not just to their role, but to a larger purpose and ecosystem.

Ultimately, belonging has never been about how much technology exists in the workplace. It is about whether people feel seen, valued, and connected to something meaningful. In fact, as work becomes more digital, that human connection becomes even more important. The future airport may be powered by algorithms, but it will continue to be sustained by people who feel a sense of purpose, pride, and belonging in what they do.

BIAL's expansion plans and its AI ambitions are both moving fast at the same time, across a workforce ecosystem of thousands of people spanning multiple employers on one campus. Which of the two is pulling harder on HR's bandwidth right now, and how are you sequencing between them?

I do not see them as competing priorities. In many ways, they are two sides of the same transformation.

Expansion creates scale. AI creates capability. To deliver a larger, more complex airport sustainably, we need both. The real challenge for HR is ensuring that growth and technology evolve together rather than on separate tracks.

As BIAL continues to expand, our focus is naturally on building leadership pipelines, strengthening critical capabilities, attracting talent, and creating career opportunities across the airport ecosystem. At the same time, AI is changing how work gets done, how decisions are made, and what skills will be most valuable in the future. If we focused only on growth, we would risk building yesterday's workforce for tomorrow's airport. If we focused only on AI, we would risk losing sight of the people and capabilities required to operate at scale.

So, our approach has been to sequence them together. Every conversation about workforce growth includes a conversation about future skills. Every discussion on technology adoption includes a discussion on capability building, leadership readiness, and employee experience.

This becomes particularly important because BIAL is not transforming a workforce within a single company. We are part of an airport ecosystem where tens of thousands of people across multiple employers contribute to the passenger experience every day. As that ecosystem grows and becomes more technology-enabled, our responsibility is to ensure that the experience evolves without losing the sense of place and human connection that underpin our Feels Like BLR philosophy, bringing together people, culture and thoughtful details to create an experience rooted in our cultural identity.

Ultimately, if I had to choose where HR is investing the most energy, it is not in expansion or AI individually. It is in ensuring that people can thrive in a future where both are happening simultaneously. The question is no longer whether the airport will grow or whether technology will advance. Both are certain. The real differentiator will be how effectively we help people adapt, grow, and succeed as those changes unfold.

Savi Khanna

BW Reporters Assistant Editor, BW Businessworld

data.title: Divya Gupta Appointed Associate Director– HR At HCLTech
data.description:
The HR professional brings experience in workforce management, succession planning and compensation across global business operations

Divya Gupta has been appointed Associate Director– Human Resources at HCLTech, effective October 2026. She brings over 16 years of experience within the organisation, having progressed through multiple HR business partnering and leadership roles since joining in February 2010. In her current responsibilities, she supports Digital Foundation Services, which has a global workforce of 30,000 employees, with a focus on talent management, succession planning, retention, compensation and workforce optimisation.

Progression Across HR Roles

Gupta has held several positions at HCLTech, including General Manager– HR, Deputy General Manager– Human Resources, Associate General Manager, Group Manager and Senior Manager – HR Business Partner. Her progression reflects experience across employee management, business partnering and strategic HR functions.

She has served as General Manager– HR since January 2025, according to her professional profile. She also held the position of Deputy General Manager – Human Resources between January 2023 and March 2025. Her other responsibilities have included supporting business units across geographies and aligning HR initiatives with operational requirements.

Managing Global Workforces

As an HR business partner, Gupta has handled workforce requirements across international operations. In an earlier role, she supported the North American geography, managing HR responsibilities for more than 13,000 employees across locations.

Her work covered compensation and performance management, succession planning, attrition analysis, talent management and cost optimisation. She also served as HR lead for the US geography of the infrastructure business, supporting a global workforce of more than 8,000 employees.

These responsibilities included manpower budgeting, productivity analysis, employee engagement, restructuring, utilisation and grievance handling. Her experience spans both employee-focused initiatives and workforce planning linked to business needs.

Compensation And Talent Planning

Gupta began her career at HCL Technologies as an HR trainee in February 2010 before moving through roles in HR operations and business partnering. As Assistant Manager– HR, she worked with the international HR team on compensation and benefits, including salary benchmarking and location-specific compensation structures.

Her responsibilities included analysing living costs and taxation across countries, assessing the feasibility of employee deployments and supporting salary decisions in coordination with employees and business leaders. She also handled employee queries relating to appraisals, transfers and international assignments.

Focus On Workforce Strategy

Gupta holds a Master of Business Administration in Human Resource and Finance from Amity University.

Her appointment adds to her responsibilities across HR leadership and workforce management at HCLTech. Her experience in succession planning, employee retention, compensation and performance management forms part of her professional background as she takes on the Associate Director – Human Resources role.

data.title: Ritesh Jha Joins KPMG India As Talent Acquisition Head
data.description:
The HR leader brings over two decades of recruitment experience across banking, financial services, technology and consulting

Ritesh Jha has joined KPMG India as Head of Talent Acquisition, bringing over 20 years of experience in recruitment strategy, technology hiring and HR leadership. His appointment follows stints at Lloyds Bank and Citi India, where he led talent acquisition and technology recruitment initiatives. His professional experience also includes FIS, Allegis Global Solutions, Info Edge India and GE, spanning recruitment delivery, workforce planning, executive hiring and talent acquisition transformation.

Experience Across Financial Services

Jha joined KPMG India in September 2026 and is based in Pune. Before this appointment, he served as Talent Acquisition Head at Lloyds Bank from October 2025 to September 2026.

Earlier, he was Senior Vice President – Technology Recruiting, Asia, at Citi India between June 2023 and October 2025. His responsibilities included global technology hiring programmes, recruitment process automation, location strategy, assessment initiatives and the development of centres of excellence for emerging technologies.

His work at Citi also covered diversity, equity and inclusion, talent branding, recruitment advisory and transformation, with coordination across regional and global teams.

Leadership Across Recruitment Functions

Before Citi India, Jha worked at FIS as TA Head for India and the Philippines and Global TA Head for its business process outsourcing division. From September 2021 to June 2023, he managed recruitment strategy and delivery across India, the Philippines and the US.

He previously served as Director – BFSI Practice, Talent Acquisition, at Allegis Global Solutions from May 2018 to September 2021. His responsibilities included scaling recruitment delivery, developing talent acquisition capabilities and advising on transformation through automation, digitisation, branding and outreach.

His earlier experience includes roles at Info Edge India and GE, adding to his exposure across technology, financial services and other sectors.

Focus On Hiring Transformation

Jha’s experience spans executive hiring, global capability centre recruitment, talent benchmarking, sourcing models, market intelligence and diversity initiatives. His professional focus includes using technology to improve recruitment delivery, talent engagement, employer branding, quality of hires and the candidate experience.

His appointment places him in charge of talent acquisition at KPMG India, where recruitment strategy and delivery form part of the organisation’s workforce requirements across business and specialist functions.

As companies navigate changing skill requirements and competition for specialised talent, recruitment leaders are increasingly involved in aligning hiring models with business needs, workforce planning and technology-led processes. Jha holds an educational qualification from Bangalore University.

data.title: Life Insurers Value Of New Business Seen Rising 10-20% In Q2FY27: Report
data.description:
Protection products are expected to support margins, while proposed changes to distribution payouts and expense limits are likely to dominate insurers’ earnings discussions

Indian life insurers are expected to report year-on-year growth of 10-20 per cent in value of new business (VNB) in the second quarter of FY27, supported by demand for protection products and steady underwriting performance, according to Kotak Institutional Equities.

The brokerage expects private life insurers under its coverage to post annualised premium equivalent (APE) growth of 10-15 per cent, with VNB rising 6-18 per cent. However, discussions around proposed regulatory changes are likely to take centre stage during earnings calls, potentially overshadowing quarterly performance.

Protection Products Support Growth

Growth in protection plans is expected to support insurers’ margins despite moderate growth in new business premiums. Kotak expects private insurers to report margin movements ranging from a 200-basis-point contraction to a 150-basis-point expansion.

Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC) is expected to outperform private peers on VNB growth, with the brokerage projecting a 40 per cent increase and a 320-basis-point expansion in VNB margin to 22.5 per cent. A higher share of non-participating products is expected to support the improvement.

Among private insurers, Axis Max Life is expected to record 14 per cent growth in both APE and VNB. SBI Life Insurance’s APE is projected to rise 14 per cent, although the loss of input tax credit following the goods and services tax exemption is expected to weigh on margins.

HDFC Life Insurance’s growth could remain moderate after APE declined 2 per cent year-on-year in July before recovering to 17 per cent growth in August. ICICI Prudential Life Insurance is expected to benefit from continued growth in protection products.

Regulatory Changes In Focus

Proposed changes to distribution payouts and expense of management (EoM) guidelines are expected to be key concerns for life insurers. The changes could affect credit protection business, distribution strategies and insurers’ dependence on bancassurance and other third-party channels.

Insurers will also need to assess the implications of potential changes to bank distribution arrangements, including open and closed architecture models. The ability to comply with revised expense limits while maintaining growth will remain an important factor for the sector.

Kotak expects near-term growth to remain supportive but cautions that FY28 could be more challenging as insurers adjust to new rules and face a higher base. Further regulatory developments, including changes to product, customer redressal and claims rules, along with the implementation of IFRS 17 and risk-based capital requirements, could influence the sector’s outlook.

data.title: Jio Platforms Targets Rs 30,200 Cr In India’s Biggest IPO
data.description:
Reliance Industries’ digital services arm targets a valuation of Rs 10.3 lakh crore, below earlier expectations, as market volatility tempers pricing ambitions

Jio Platforms is targeting a fundraise of about Rs 30,200 crore through its initial public offering (IPO), with a reported price band of Rs 1,065-1,119 per share, according to media reports.

The Reliance Industries subsidiary plans to open subscriptions on 21 October, with listing expected on 28 October. The schedule and pricing remain subject to change.

The proposed offering could surpass Hyundai Motor India’s Rs 27,800-crore IPO in October 2024 to become India’s largest-ever public issue. At the reported price band, Jio Platforms is targeting a valuation of up to Rs 10.3 lakh crore, equivalent to about USD 106 billion, according to media reports.

The proposed valuation is below some earlier estimates as a sell-off in Indian equities has tempered pricing expectations for IPOs.

Price Band And Issue Size

Jio Platforms plans to price its shares between Rs 1,065 and Rs 1,119 apiece, according to media reports. At the upper end of the range, the company could raise approximately Rs 30,200 crore, based on Bloomberg’s calculations.

The proposed issue comprises up to 270 million new shares, equivalent to about 2.93 per cent of the company’s post-issue equity capital, according to Bloomberg’s calculations based on the draft prospectus filed in June. Assuming the full 270 million shares are issued, the proceeds would amount to Rs 28,755 crore at the lower end and Rs 30,213 crore at the upper end of the reported price band.

The subscription window is expected to run from 21 October to 23 October, with the anchor investor book scheduled to open on 19 October. The shares are expected to begin trading on 28 October, cited media reports. The company has not finalised all the terms, and the dates, valuation and price range could change.

Valuation Below Earlier Expectations

The proposed valuation of up to Rs 10.3 lakh crore is below some of the estimates discussed earlier for Jio Platforms. Bloomberg reported that the company had previously been expected to seek a valuation of around Rs 11 lakh crore, while valuations floated earlier ranged from USD 130 billion to USD 170 billion.

In June, Motilal Oswal Financial Services estimated Jio Platforms’ valuation at USD 115 billion to USD 118 billion, while Dolat Capital valued the company at about USD 110 billion, according to media reports. These are analyst estimates rather than the final valuation for the IPO.

The change in expectations comes amid a sell-off in Indian equities, which has tempered pricing expectations for several prospective public offerings, Bloomberg reported. The final valuation will depend on the price and terms at which the company proceeds with the issue.

Jio Platforms’ proposed fundraising would exceed Hyundai Motor India’s Rs 27,800-crore IPO in October 2024, which remains the previous record for an Indian public issue. The size of the proposed Jio offering would make it a significant test of investor demand for large share sales.

The IPO would also give public-market investors a direct investment route into Reliance Industries’ telecommunications and digital services business. Jio Platforms operates in areas including mobile connectivity and digital services, while its parent company has interests across multiple sectors.

Nineteen Banks Appointed For Share Sale

Jio Platforms has appointed 19 banks to work on the proposed offering, according to Bloomberg. The institutions include Kotak Mahindra Capital, Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, Axis Capital, BNP Paribas and Citigroup.

The price band, valuation and timetable remain provisional until the relevant details are formally confirmed.

data.title: Canara HSBC Life Insurance Reports 17.3% Premium Growth In H1 FY27
data.description:
New business premiums rise 16.1 per cent, while value of new business grows 24 per cent as protection products gain traction

Canara HSBC Life Insurance reported a 17.3 per cent year-on-year increase in total premium income to Rs 4,742 crore in the first half of FY27, supported by growth in new business and renewals.

New business premium income rose 16.1 per cent to Rs 1,984 crore, while renewal premiums increased 18.2 per cent to Rs 2,758 crore. Annualised premium equivalent (APE), a measure of new business sales, grew 14.4 per cent to Rs 1,250 crore during the six months ended 30 September 2026.

New Business And Protection Drive Growth

The insurer’s value of new business (VNB) increased 24 per cent to Rs 266 crore, with a VNB margin of 21.3 per cent. Profit after tax rose 10.8 per cent to Rs 71.2 crore.

Protection business recorded 44 per cent growth, with protection APE reaching Rs 131 crore and accounting for 10.5 per cent of total APE. The company also reported continued momentum in credit life and annuity products.

Individual weighted premium income increased 14.5 per cent to Rs 1,117 crore. Assets under management grew 13.9 per cent year-on-year to Rs 50,200 crore as of 30 September 2026.

Traditional Products Gain Share

The product mix shifted towards traditional savings products during the period, reflecting customer preferences and volatility in equity markets. Unit-linked insurance plans (ULIPs) accounted for 41 per cent of APE, down from 50 per cent in H1 FY26. The share of non-participating savings products rose to around 25 per cent from 17 per cent.

The insurer’s embedded value stood at Rs 7,622 crore at the end of September, with an operating return on embedded value of 19.8 per cent on a rolling 12-month basis. Its solvency ratio was 180 per cent, above the regulatory minimum of 150 per cent.

Canara HSBC Life’s board has also approved raising Rs 287.5 crore through non-convertible debentures on a private placement basis. The proposed fundraising is intended to support business expansion, investments in distribution and solvency requirements as the protection portfolio grows.

data.title: Portugal state buys 5.3% REN stake, lifting holding to 19%
data.description:
Portugal's state holding company Parpublica has agreed to buy a 5.3% stake in power and gas grid operator REN from insurer Fidelidade, controlled by China's Fosun , completing the government's push to rebuild a strategic stake in REN that has now reached 19%.

  • In August, the state bought a 13.7% stake in REN, marking its return to the company after a 12-year hiatus. The government said then it aimed to increase the stake to as much as 20%.

  • China's State Grid is REN's largest shareholder with a 25% stake.

  • Portugal's Finance Ministry said in a statement late on Friday that the acquisition was intended to "defend the public interest and preserve a strategic asset for the country", adding that the "government considered its objective in REN achieved."

  • The government did not disclose the value of the deal, but based on REN's market value, the 5.3% stake is worth roughly 125 million euros ($140 million).

  • The acquisition is in line with Prime Minister Luis Montenegro's plan, announced in June, to create a sovereign wealth fund holding stakes in strategically important companies.

  • A Fidelidade spokesperson said its stake in REN had always been primarily a financial investment, and the decision to sell it was driven, among other reasons, by the asset's more than 40% increase in value over the past two years.

($1 = 0.8927 euros)

data.title: Shubhankar Sharma retains his lead at Kapil Dev Invitational Tour Championship
data.description:
Greater Noida, Oct. 10 -- Shubhankar Sharma returned an even-par 72 to retain a two-shot lead after the third round of the Rs 2 crore Kapil Dev Invitational Tour Championship at the Jaypee Greens Golf & Spa Resort in Greater Noida.

The 30-year-old Chandigarh golfer (68-65-72), who began the day with a four-stroke advantage, mixed five birdies with three bogeys and a double bogey to remain at 11-under 205 heading into the final round, according to a press release from the Kapil Dev Invitational Tour Championship.

Bengaluru's Manoj S (70-71-66) and Italy's Michele Ortolani (72-70-65) emerged as Shubhankar's closest challengers at nine-under 207.

"The back nine was disappointing because I missed a few opportunities coming in and dropped some shots. However, I'm still playing good golf and have plenty to look forward to tomorrow. Hopefully, I can carry the momentum from today's front nine through all 18 holes in the final round."

data.title: Crypto’s 10/10 Trauma: Did Traders Really Deleverage Before the Anniversary?
data.description:
Crypto traders took on more borrowed money heading into the 10/10 anniversary, not less. That left them exposed when Bitcoin slid toward $80,000 and over $1 billion in bets were forcibly closed.

On October 10, 2025, a tariff threat from President Donald Trump set off more than $19 billion in forced closures, a record. This week, some traders claimed fear of a repeat had pushed the market to cut risk.

“The bear market PTSD is so strong that people actually deleveraged for an anniversary to a liquidation event. Think how deep that PTSD goes if you’re doing that. I’m telling you, there is mass under exposure and things actually look good,” said Eric Conner, a crypto veteran and one of the co-authors of EIP-1559.

But did they?

Borrowed Bets Rose Into Bitcoin’s Drop

Leverage means trading with borrowed money. If prices move the wrong way, exchanges close the position automatically, which is called a liquidation.

That peak landed on the day of the selloff. Bitcoin fell to $80,393, and over $1 billion was liquidated in 24 hours, as BeInCrypto reported. About $930 million came from bets on rising prices.

BeInCrypto flagged the risk a day earlier. Its 10/10 repeat analysis found the market carried nearly as much leverage for its size as before last year’s crash.

CryptoQuant’s Estimated Leverage Ratio compares open bets with the Bitcoin held on exchanges. A higher reading means more borrowing. It climbed from about 0.234 on October 3 to roughly 0.256 on October 8.

The ratio has since eased only to about 0.250, still above the week’s start.

However, total open bets fell from about $154 billion to roughly $142 billion, CoinGlass data shows.

Funding Costs Fall Far Below 2025 as the Fear Gauge Holds at Greed

Funding rates are fees that traders betting on gains pay to those betting on losses. High fees signal a crowded bullish side.

Deribit’s Bitcoin funding rate stood near 7.1% annualized this week, against 26.9% before the 2025 crash. On OKX, funding averaged about 3.5% over the past seven days, exchange data shows.

Alternative.me’s Fear and Greed Index scores sentiment from zero to 100. It read 64, or “greed,” on Saturday and dipped only to 59 during the Friday selloff.

Bitcoin trades at $82,699, up 0.14% in 24 hours, according to BeInCrypto data. That leaves it about 35% below its October 2025 record near $126,000. Glassnode data places the next cluster of leveraged bets near $75,000.

data.title: US PERM Freeze May Squeeze Indian IT Margins By 30 Bps
data.description:
The suspension of green card-related labour certifications could raise employee retention and hiring costs, even as Indian IT companies reduce their reliance on US work visas

Indian IT services companies could face operating margin pressure of 10–30 basis points over the next 12 months following the US suspension of a key employment-based green card process. The impact is expected to stem from higher talent retention and workforce costs rather than an immediate loss of revenue.

The US Department of Labour’s October 8 decision to suspend Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) processing for eight technology companies has increased uncertainty for Indian IT services firms and their employees. While the move affects a route to permanent residency for foreign workers, companies have increasingly relied on local hiring and offshore delivery to reduce their dependence on immigration programmes.

Industry estimates suggest the financial impact could deepen if the suspension continues for several years. However, the near-term implications will depend on how affected companies manage employee retention, local recruitment and delivery costs.

Margin Pressure Could Build Over Time

According to media reports, the suspension could put operating margins under pressure by 10–30 basis points over the next 12 months. If the restrictions persist for several years, the pressure could increase to 30 to 75 basis points, while revenues could be 0.25 to 0.75 per cent below the levels otherwise expected.

The estimates indicate that the immediate impact on revenue could be negligible, with the principal risk arising from additional workforce-related expenses. Companies may need to offer stronger retention incentives, increase local hiring or rely more on subcontractors to maintain delivery commitments.

These are industry estimates rather than company-specific earnings forecasts. The actual impact will depend on the number of affected employees, the duration of the restrictions and the measures companies take to manage their US operations.

US Suspends PERM Processing For Eight Companies

The US administration announced the suspension on 8 October, covering Indian IT services companies Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech, Cognizant and Capgemini, along with US technology companies Microsoft and Adobe.

The US Department of Labour said it would stop accepting new applications and processing pending PERM applications involving the affected employers while investigations into alleged programme abuse continue. PERM certification is a key step in the employment-based green card process, requiring employers to demonstrate that qualified US workers are not available for the relevant position under applicable rules.

The suspension does not, by itself, amount to a blanket ban on H-1B visas. However, it creates uncertainty for employees seeking permanent residency through affected employers, particularly those whose immigration plans depend on the certification process.

Local Hiring And Offshore Delivery May Limit The Impact

Indian IT companies have reduced their dependence on employment-based immigration routes over the years, expanding local recruitment in the US and shifting more work to offshore delivery centres. This transition could limit the immediate effect of the suspension on their operations and earnings.

TCS, for instance, said its US workforce strategy would remain unaffected, citing the limited number of PERM applications it had submitted in the preceding two years. The company has also outlined plans to hire an additional 15,000 employees in the US over the next five years.

Nevertheless, according to media reports, analysts have flagged longer-term risks around talent retention, regulatory uncertainty and the potential for higher recruitment costs. Any extension of US scrutiny to other immigration or wage-related rules could add to those pressures.

Longer-Term Risks Extend Beyond Margins

The financial consequences will depend partly on whether the suspension remains limited to PERM processing or is followed by wider restrictions affecting foreign-worker recruitment. A prolonged freeze could make it harder for affected employees to secure permanent residency through their current employers, increasing the challenge of retaining experienced professionals.

For Indian IT companies, the issue is therefore not limited to the immediate cost of compliance. Higher employee turnover, replacement hiring and changes to workforce deployment could affect delivery economics over time. The estimated margin impact remains contingent on how the situation develops and how companies adjust their staffing strategies.

data.title: India’s Retail Inflation May Rise To 5.47% On Food Prices
data.description:
Union Bank of India expects food inflation to accelerate to 7.35 per cent, driven by surging vegetable and onion prices, supply disruptions and below-average monsoon rainfall

India’s retail inflation is projected to rise to 5.47 per cent in September 2026 from 4.82 per cent in August, driven by a sharp increase in food prices, according to a report by Union Bank of India (UBI).

The projected increase would take headline inflation to its highest level since December 2024 and above the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) 4 per cent medium-term target, the report said.

Food inflation is estimated to have accelerated to 7.35 per cent in September from 5.66 per cent in August, with vegetables accounting for a significant share of the increase. Vegetable inflation is projected to jump to 9.34 per cent from 0.99 per cent a month earlier.

Onion prices rose by around 34 per cent during September, according to data from the Department of Consumer Affairs cited in the report. Inflationary pressures also extended to cereals, pulses, sugar, edible oils and milk.

Food Prices Face Weather And Supply Pressures

UBI attributed the expected increase in inflation to prolonged supply disruptions, higher energy costs, rising global chip prices and the potential effects of a strong El Niño weather phenomenon.

The southwest monsoon ended the June-September 2026 season with rainfall 13 per cent below the long-period average. Reservoir levels stood at 72 per cent, compared with 92 per cent a year earlier, potentially adding to agricultural supply pressures.

Total kharif crop sowing was around 1 per cent lower than the previous year, while paddy sowing declined by nearly 3 per cent.

The report noted that food inflation had risen from 2.12 per cent in January 2026 to 5.66 per cent in August, reflecting persistent price pressures despite a favourable base effect from the previous year.

Core Inflation Also Edges Higher

Price pressures are expected to extend beyond food, with core inflation, which excludes more volatile components, projected to increase marginally to 4.48 per cent in September from 4.44 per cent in August.

The broad-based rise suggests that supply-side shocks and higher input costs are increasingly feeding into the wider inflation basket.

The inflation outlook will remain sensitive to food supply conditions, energy prices and weather developments in the coming months, as policymakers assess the implications for household purchasing power and monetary policy.

data.title: FIIs Sell Rs 30,294 Cr Of Equities; DIIs Match Outflows With Buying
data.description:
Foreign investors purchase shares worth Rs 10,373.99 crore and sell Rs 13,942.89 crore on Friday

Foreign institutional investors (FIIs) remained net sellers of Indian equities throughout the week ended October 9, offloading shares worth Rs 30,294 crore, while domestic institutional investors (DIIs) stepped up purchases to absorb much of the selling pressure, provisional exchange data showed.

DIIs recorded net purchases of Rs 30,313 crore over the week, marginally exceeding the net outflows from foreign investors. The contrasting flows came as benchmark indices broke an eight-week losing streak, with a sharp rally on Friday helping the Sensex and Nifty recover ground.

On Friday, FIIs sold equities worth Rs 3,568.90 crore on a net basis, while DIIs bought shares worth Rs 4,743.26 crore. This left the market with net institutional buying of Rs 1,174.36 crore for the session.

Foreign investors purchased shares worth Rs 10,373.99 crore and sold Rs 13,942.89 crore on Friday. Domestic institutions bought equities worth Rs 15,626.53 crore and sold Rs 10,883.27 crore.

“Going ahead, relentless FII selling and global headwinds are likely to keep markets volatile, though record domestic institutional buying should continue to limit the downside. Market participants will closely track US and Indian inflation data, US bond yields, Brent crude prices and developments in US-Iran geopolitical tensions in the coming week,” said Pabitro Mukherjee, Deputy Vice President-Research, Bajaj Broking.

Domestic Buying Counters Persistent Foreign Selling

Foreign investors were net sellers in all five trading sessions during the week, with the heaviest outflow of Rs 12,943.58 crore recorded on October 8. Domestic institutions provided a counterweight, posting their strongest net buying of Rs 10,703.11 crore on the same day.

Across the week, FIIs bought shares worth Rs 65,610.73 crore and sold Rs 95,904.02 crore. DIIs purchased equities worth Rs 95,434.53 crore and sold Rs 65,122.06 crore.

The data highlight the extent to which domestic institutional demand has helped offset persistent foreign selling, even as market sentiment remains sensitive to global developments and the outlook for corporate earnings.

Sensex, Nifty End 8-week Losing Streak

Indian benchmark indices ended their eight-week run of losses, with the Sensex and Nifty gaining nearly 1 per cent each over the week. The Nifty Bank index advanced more than 1 per cent, while the midcap index finished largely unchanged.

The recovery was uneven across sectors. Metal, realty and power stocks were among the weakest performers, with sectoral indices declining by as much as 4 per cent. Capital markets, fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) and public sector banks led the gains, rising by up to 3 per cent.

On the Nifty, 30 constituents ended the week lower, with losses extending to 7 per cent. Adani Enterprises, Max Healthcare, JSW Steel, Hindalco Industries and Bharat Electronics were among the biggest laggards.

Trent, BSE, Kotak Mahindra Bank, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Bharti Airtel and ITC featured among the leading gainers.

While domestic institutional purchases helped stabilise the market, the persistence of foreign outflows remains a key factor for investors to monitor as equities attempt to sustain their recovery.

data.title: Keurig Reimagines Coffee Without the Plastic. Don't Worry, Your K-Cup Still Lives. — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Liz Moyer

Nearly 30 years after Keurig introduced the world to single-serve coffee pods, the company, now part of Keurig Dr Pepper, is going pod-free.

Well, actually, it is rolling out a line of single-serve coffee rounds made entirely of compressed grounds and encased in a seaweed-based coating to hold it together during shipping. The company sees this format, which resembles a mini hockey puck, as the future of its coffee business. K-Cup lovers need not be alarmed: they will stick around for now.

The new brand, which it calls Alta Rounds, was inspired by customer interest in barista-style coffee options for home brewing but with less waste. Keurig has caught a lot of criticism over the years over that last issue.

Since the K-Cup single serve brewing pod was introduced in 1998, Keurig has produced billions and billions of them — by some estimates at least 10 billion K-Cups are produced annually, though the company doesn't release that number.

Though these small plastic cups are made of recyclable material, many residential recycling sorting centers aren't equipped to handle them. Keurig actually paid $1.5 million in a civil penalty to the Securities and Exchange Commission in 2024 after accusations it made inaccurate statements about the K-Cup's recyclability.

Still, Keurig executives say their coffee and brewing machines are used in 47 million homes, and this latest iteration of the single-serve concept was driven by the need to outwit the competition.

"We've grown into a disrupter in the coffee category," Phil Drapeau, the senior vice president of future coffee systems for Keurig, said at a recent event in New York where Keurig employees demonstrated the Alta Rounds and the new machine Keurig built to brew them at home. "We needed to break free from the constraints of the K-Cup system."

Keurig Dr Pepper is months away from the formal separation of its businesses into a beverage company and a coffee business. No doubt the Alta Rounds are part of what it hopes will be the growth story for the new stand-alone Global Coffee Co., which has a new CEO, Russ Torres, joining from Kimberly-Clark.

Keurig has estimated the coffee company can generate about $16 billion in annual revenue. The split, planned for early 2027, comes after it bought JDE Peet in a bid to create a global coffee leader.

Market data company Numerator says Keurig Dr Pepper leads its competitors in branded coffee pod manufacturers, reaching 21.3% of U.S. households, ahead of Nestlé (16.5%) and J.M. Smucker (14.4%). Keurig's share of coffee pod spending increased from 19.5% to 19.8% in the latest year — though is still below 2024 levels.

But more broadly, coffee pod household penetration is dropping, suggesting people are buying coffee in other forms. Keurig's own U.S. coffee organic sales growth has been slowing, notes Barclays analyst Lauren Lieberman, who has an Overweight rating on the stock.

Lieberman says the merger with Peet showcased the merits of the more diversified combination compared with legacy Keurig going it alone.

As for Alta Rounds, Keurig is currently taking orders for a $500 bundle that includes the brewing machine, four boxes of the coffee rounds (which come in six varieties and have eight rounds a box), and glassware to go with it.

The pressed coffee rounds can withstand the extra pressure the new machine uses while brewing. K-Cups would burst under the same pressure. When Keurig began developing the product six years ago, it drew inspiration from the grounds that a barista tamps down in an espresso maker before turning on the machine. The Alta Round feels damp and spongy after brewing but holds its shape.

Product developers and engineers tried various shapes over the years and ultimately settled on a disk. Then they experimented with various coatings and settled on an algae-based formula made from seaweed harvested off the coast of France. It doesn't have a taste and can be composted, along with the grounds themselves.

Ultimately Peet's coffee will become part of the Alta coffee collection as the brand scales up. The new Alta brewing machines can also brew K-Cups from a separate compartment. (Older Keurig brewers cannot accept Alta Rounds, however.)

Drapeau acknowledges that it's going to take time to build the business beyond the novelty it is now. For now Keurig is taking a hybrid approach, with the new pod-less coffee and the familiar K-Cups.

"We're going to get better," he said.

data.title: Nutritious midnight snacks approved by dieticians
data.description:
New Delhi, Oct. 10 -- What's your favourite midnight snack? it's a question that regularly pops up on celebrity rapid-fire rounds, romanticising relishing everything from instant noodles to chocolates, and all forms of indulgent foods. Pop culture has embraced the trope of crying buckets into tubs of ice cream in the night after a bad day or a breakup. Late-night eating has always been packaged as comfort and even a little rebellion. And admittedly, there is something appealing about it: a favourite snack in a quiet house with dim lights feels like a small reward.

But, dieticians advise keeping a gap of two-three hours before bed and recommend 7pm as the cut-out time for dinner. In an ideal world without late-night pickle-ball matches, parties and PMS, this would have been possible. But, plans change, routines get disrupted and life gets in the way. Reaching for a midnight snack occasionally is not alarming, and you can't sleep with a grumbling tummy. So, if you are starving at midnight, what can you eat without guilt? It depends on what kind of night you've had, and experts talk about being aware of hunger cues while sharing a list of nourishing foods that won't disrupt your health.

A sweet tooth caused due to PMS or hormonal changes can feel impossible to ignore. In such a case, the idea isn't to ban the treat, but also not to let a midnight craving turn into a midnight feast.

"Our abilities to make decisions and exercise self-control decrease when we are physically and mentally exhausted. This makes us surrender to our cravings, especially at nights, as the intake of sweet foods can stimulate the brain pathways involved in reward response and provide comfort, pleasure, and relief to us," notes Dietician Niranjana Surendran, Clinical Dietitian, Rainbow Children's Hospital, Bengaluru.

REACH FOR: One or two dates with toned milk, a small piece of sesame-ajwain jaggery chikki, dark chocolate with almonds or peanut butter with apple or banana.

If you need a small bite after squeezing in a late workout, a protein-rich snack to support muscle recovery and replenish your energy levels makes more sense than raiding the biscuit tin.

Dietician Divya Jain, Senior Dietician, CK Birla Hospitals, Jaipur, suggests choosing foods that provide protein, fibre and healthy fats. "When eating late, the goal is to supply your muscles with protein for repair while keeping carbs light and fibre moderate so your digestion doesn't disrupt sleep," she advises.

REACH FOR: Greek yogurt, cottage cheese, hard-boiled egg or scrambled whites, protein shake (whey or plant-based), a handful of almonds or walnuts.

For new parents, midnight eating can be less about indulgence and more about being exhausted and hungry. And when you are running on broken sleep and have a newborn to tend to, it's easy to reach for whatever is quickest. Stocking up on healthy snacks and drinks is essential.

"After a mentally draining day, the body requires consolation. Several palatable foods with high amounts of sugar, fats or salt provide immediate gratification but result in an energy crash afterwards," says Dietician Deepti Lokeshappa, Senior Consultant, Nutritionist and Dietitian, Motherhood Hospital, Bengaluru. "To avoid this, just be mindful of your choices and keep healthy snacks handy."

REACH FOR: Methi-gond-date-wheat laddoos, a boiled egg with a few whole-grain crackers, a glass of warm milk, or a handful of nuts.

The festive season is here and late-night hang-outs are bound to happen. Don't order that pizza or reach for those cup noodles on impulse as your cravings for calorie-rich comfort food could be caused by the delay in your bedtime. "Erratic sleeping habits can lead to eating during the late hours of the day and over time, this could turn into an established craving or a habit of eating even if you are not really hungry physiologically," points out Dietician Aditi Prasad Apte, Senior - Clinical Nutritionist, Aster RV Hospital, Bengaluru. Wait for a while to see if you are actually hungry and opt for something very light and easily digestible, she recommends.

REACH FOR: Roasted Bengal gram, roasted unsalted peanuts, puffed rice (with roasted peanuts, drops of mustard oil and chaat masala).

The exhaustion is real, but sleep continues to evade you. And somewhere between scrolling, watching television and staring at the ceiling, the urge to order a burger on Zomato can creep in. But first ask yourself: Am I hungry, or am I eating just because I am awake and bored?

"Sleep and appetite are closely interconnected. Eventually, the person may experience a learned craving or habit cue even without significant physiological hunger," says Jain highlighting the significance of body awareness. "However, if your stomach is genuinely empty, going to bed hungry can also keep you awake. Choose a small and easy-to- digest snack (100-150 calories) that promotes sleep."

REACH FOR: Banana with 1 tsp almond butter, a glass of warm milk or oat milk, a handful of tart cherries or walnuts, roasted Bengal gram, raw paneer cubes sprinkled with salt and pepper.

Deepa Natarajan Lobo is an independent journalist based in Bengaluru.

data.title: OTPless Appoints Former BharatPe Technology Head Geetanshu Singla As CTO
data.description:
Bengaluru-based identity and access management startup OTPless has appointed former BharatPe technology head and Genwise co-founder Geetanshu Singla as its Chief Technology Officer (CTO), as per a media report.

In his new role, Singla will oversee engineering, product development, platform architecture, reliability and security across OTPless’s authentication and fraud prevention systems. These include Silent Network Authentication, WhatsApp authentication, device intelligence and passkeys.

Singla previously served as Vice President of Technology at BharatPe, where he worked closely with OTPless co-founders Satyam Nathani and Tanmay Sagar during the fintech company’s early growth. He later co-founded Genwise, which shut down operations in December last year.

The appointment follows a series of leadership changes at OTPless. On 18 September, the company elevated Nathani to the position of Chief Executive Officer (CEO) and Sagar to Chief Operating Officer (COO). On October 1, it appointed early team member Manas Poddar as Chief Business Officer (CBO).

OTPless claims to authenticate more than 300 million users across consumer platforms, including Meesho, Zepto, Navi, PhysicsWallah, ShareChat, Shiprocket and ixigo. The company has grown its topline 2.5 times over the past year, reaching annualised revenue of Rs 36 crore. It has also reported break-even performance over the past two quarters.

The businesses we serve are some of India’s largest consumer platforms, and for them, login is the front door to their entire business. A failed or slow authentication is a lost customer, so they need technology they can rely on at any scale, on any day. Geetanshu has built and run technology at unicorn scale, and his joining strengthens the technical trust our customers place in us, said Sagar.

Singla said he had worked closely with Nathani and Sagar during his time at BharatPe and described joining OTPless as coming back home. He added that the company’s expansion from OTP authentication to a broader identity and trust layer presented a significant opportunity.

Founded in 2023, OTPless provides authentication and identity infrastructure to consumer internet companies. Its platform enables user verification through Silent Network Authentication, WhatsApp authentication, device intelligence and passkeys, reducing reliance on SMS-based one-time passwords.

The company has raised more than USD 6 million from investors, including Venture Highway, White Venture, FJ Labs, SIDBI and Piper Serica.

data.title: Are you an NRI renting out property in India? Here is who can help to manage it; how to pay tax and remit money abroad
data.description:
New Delhi, Oct. 10 -- Non-resident Indians (NRIs) can legally own and rent out property in India, whether it is a family home they inherited, an investment flat they have purchased or a house they chose to keep after moving abroad.

Renting out such property can provide a steady income while also ensuring that it remains occupied and maintained.

However, managing a rental property from abroad can be challenging, particularly when it comes to handling tenants and repairs, collecting rent, completing documentation and complying with tax rules.

Here is what NRI property owners need to know about managing rent, getting professional assistance and repatriating rental income.

An NRI can let out their property in India by using online rent agreements, digital tenant verification, e-stamping and a non-resident ordinary (NRO) bank account for rent collection, which can be further remitted abroad.

Tenants can transfer the rent amount through NEFT, IMPS, or UPI linked to the NRO account. Many landlords also set up automatic reminders or use a property manager to follow up on payment dates.

Funds in an NRO account are partially repatriable up to $1 million per financial year, subject to applicable conditions and payment of taxes where required. The house owner must also keep rent collection consistent and documented to make the repatriation process easier.

Many people may wonder if they can receive rent in their non-resident external (NRE) account instead as funds maintained in it can be fully repatriated outside India. However, Indian residents cannot make direct payments or deposit local funds into a NRE account.

In the event the tenant is an NRI or a person of Indian origin (PIO), only then the landlord can receive rent for immovable property in their NRE account, according to a blog post by ICICI Bank.

NRIs have several options for managing rental property in India, depending on how much assistance they need and how frequently they can oversee the property themselves.

A trusted family member or friend can handle basic tasks like coordinating with tenants, handing over keys and arranging repairs. Such a representative can be appointed through a Power of Attorney (POA) to carry out specified legal and administrative tasks on the NRI's behalf.

Alternatively, a property management company can handle day-to-day responsibilities, including finding tenants, collecting rent and coordinating maintenance. This option can be considered if you cannot appoint a POA or need professional assistance.

Some NRIs combine these options. For instance, a property manager may handle daily operations, while a POA holder signs the rent agreement or completes other formalities that require the owner's authorisation.

Rental income earned by a non-resident Indian (NRI) from property in India is taxable under the head 'Income from house property' at the applicable income-tax slab rates. NRIs can claim a deduction for municipal taxes paid during the financial year, along with the standard deduction of 30% of the net annual value, while calculating taxable rental income.

Under Section 195 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, rent paid to an NRI is generally subject to Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) at the applicable rates, including surcharge and cess, wherever applicable. The final tax liability depends on the individual's taxable income and the applicable tax provisions.

As an NRI, you may also consult your tax advisor to analyse relevant Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) to claim any benefit on such rental income available under such agreement.

data.title: Sam Altman-backed Bitcoin life insurer, Meanwhile, raises more funds
data.description:
Meanwhile, a life insurer licensed to operate completely in Bitcoin, announced $37.5 million in new funding from existing investors.

Bermuda-based Meanwhile, whose backers include OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, has now raised more than $180 million.

Bain Capital Crypto led the new round, alongside Haun Ventures, Framework Ventures, Pantera Capital, Apollo, Northwestern Mutual Future Ventures, and Morgan Creek Digital, it said in a statement.

The round follows increased international demand for Meanwhile’s Bitcoin life insurance policies, particularly in Asia, Europe and the Middle East, amid broader macro instability, according to the statement.

“Wealthy families around the world already hold Bitcoin. What they haven’t had is a regulated way to pass it on,” Zac Townsend, Meanwhile’s co-founder and CEO, said in the statement. “Brokers came to us because their clients kept asking. This round lets us keep up with them.”

Passing Bitcoin to the next generation

In early 2026, Meanwhile launched BTC Life 1-Pay, a single-premium whole life policy built for high-net-worth clients outside the United States. It is the company’s second product line after BTC 10-Pay, which is designed for US taxpayers.

Policies can be owned by individuals, trusts or companies, which makes them a fit for succession and estate planning, the company said.

Net long-term underwriting income has already passed last year’s total and is on track to more than double in 2026, the company added, without revealing precise figures.

Cointelegraph reported in June that WTW, a global insurance broker and risk advisory company, had acquired crypto insurance platform Redefind and launched a digital asset protection service that covers expenses related to forensic investigations, asset tracing and legal recovery efforts following theft or loss.

Redefind is a crypto insurance platform that allows individuals and institutions to purchase coverage for digital assets held across different custody arrangements. The company said its system uses cryptographic proof of ownership to verify insured assets.
